migrationNotes: Spine: a car park barrier program grows. It first chooses a fee (if chain), then totals a day's fees (for, range, accumulator), then admits cars until it is full (while), then combines tests (and, or, not, and & on bits), and the last screen assembles the whole program.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): python-conditions-and-loops-hook (the 2-hour stay, covered by the opener's fee bands and the first screen) and python-conditions-and-loops-why-zero stays as the self-explanation on the worked example.
Figures: the fee chain, the accumulator and the while loop figures moved from the practice screens onto the teaching screens that explain them.

lesson.title: Control which work happens

lead.text: Start with one car. The car park rewards regulars, and the program keeps a driver's visits this month in a name called units. A driver with 10 or more visits pays a fee of 0. A driver with 5 or more pays £2, and everyone else pays £4. To pick between those, the program asks questions with a yes-or-no answer. In Python such a question is called a condition. The condition units >= 10 is True when units is 10 or more and False otherwise.

Python writes a comparison with two equals signs. A single equals sign stores a value, so units = 5 sets units to 5, while units == 5 asks whether it already is 5. The conditions go into an if chain. Its first line is if units >= 10:, the middle line is elif units >= 5: (short for 'else if'), and the last is else:, which has no condition and takes whatever is left. Each of these, with the indented lines under it, is a branch. Python tests from the top, runs the first branch whose condition is True and skips the rest. Step through two drivers.

afterFigure.text: With units = 3 both tests fail, so else runs and the fee is 4. With units = 12 the first test passes, the fee is 0 and the other tests are never looked at. The order matters whenever ranges overlap. A driver with 12 visits also satisfies units >= 5, so the test for 10 has to come first. Put the narrowest condition at the top, or it never gets its turn.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

lead.text: Two lines in the chain can look alike and do different jobs. Read the line units = 5 the way Python reads it.
Follow the chain from the top for a driver with 7 visits. Stop at the first condition that holds.

That settles one car. At closing time the program has a list of the day's fees and needs their total. A for loop does the repeating. It takes a collection of items and runs its indented lines once for each, giving each item in turn a name, so for fee in fees: runs once with fee set to the first fee and again with the second, until the items run out. Often the items are just a run of numbers, and range makes those. range(1, 6) hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. It includes its start and stops before its stop value, the rule slices follow, so 6 is never given out. A third number sets the step: range(3, 12, 3) gives 3, 6 and 9.

To add things up, the loop needs somewhere to keep the running figure. A name that starts at 0 before the loop and grows inside it is called an accumulator. With total = 0 above the loop and total += item inside it, each pass adds one more item to whatever total already holds. Starting at 0 means the first item is added to nothing, so after the first pass the total is exactly that item. Step through two totals.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the items are 0, 1, 2 and 3, and total finishes at 6. In the second, range(1, 8, 2) gives 1, 3, 5 and 7, and total finishes at 16. When all you need is the total, Python's built-in sum does the whole job in one call: sum(range(1, 5)) gives 10.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
items = list(range(4))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
items = list(range(1, 8, 2))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

lead.text: Before adding anything up, make sure you know which values range hands out.

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(1, 6): total += item.

lead.text: Work through one complete total, from the first pass to the last.

workedSteps.text: range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The stop, 6, is excluded.
total starts at 0, then grows by each item.

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(3, 12, 3): total += item.

lead.text: This time you fill in two of the lines yourself.

workedSteps.text: range(3, 12, 3) starts at 3 and steps by 3. It stops before 12. How many times does the loop run?
The items are 3, 6 and 9. Add them to total. What is total at the end?

lead.text: A for loop knows how many passes it has, because its items are counted out in advance. Sometimes the program cannot know. The car park keeps letting cars in until it is full, and nobody can say beforehand how many that will take. For that Python has the while loop. It is written as while followed by a condition, and it tests the condition before every pass. If the test gives True, the indented lines run and the test is made again. When it gives False, the loop ends and the program carries on below it.

The lines inside have to change something the condition looks at. Otherwise the test gives the same answer for ever and the loop never finishes. In the picture, count starts at 1 and the loop runs while count < 6. Each pass adds to count and adds 1 to turns, which counts the passes. Step through both cases and compare.

afterFigure.text: With count += 2 the values are 3, 5 and 7, so turns finishes at 3. With count += 3 they are 4 and 7, so turns finishes at 2. In the first case the test still gave True at 5, so one more pass ran and carried count past the limit. The test happens only before a pass, never during one.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 2
    turns += 1

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 3
    turns += 1

lead.text: Test the condition before each pass and write down the value count takes. Stop when a test gives False.

Real fee rules seldom hang on one test. A night rate might apply only to a car that arrived after 18:00 and left before 06:00. Python joins tests with three words. and gives True only when both sides are True. or gives True when at least one side is. not turns True into False and False into True. Each side is worked out first and gives True or False. The word then combines those two answers. With x = 6, the test x > 3 and x < 9 asks whether x lies between 3 and 9, and the answer is True.

The symbols & and | look like and and or. On whole numbers they work on binary digits instead. Binary writes a number using only 1 and 0, in columns worth 4, 2 and 1. The number 6 is one 4 and one 2, so it is 110. The number 3 is one 2 and one 1, so it is 011. The operator & compares the columns and keeps a 1 only where both numbers have one. Here only the middle column has two 1s, which leaves 010, the number 2. Use the words for conditions and keep the symbols for work on bits.
Work out each of the three tests for x = 6 on its own before you count how many are True.

The barrier program can now be written out as it was first described. It sets total = 0 and runs a for loop over the day's stays. Inside the loop an if chain picks the fee for that stay, and total += fee adds it to the day's takings. When the stays run out, total holds the answer. A loop with a chain inside it is the shape of most data work, since data arrives as a long list of rows and the question to ask of each row usually depends on a test.

Each tool answers a different need. An if chain picks one path. A for loop repeats over items you already have. A while loop repeats until a test gives False, and the words and, or and not let one test hold several requirements. The program is complete, but the fee rule now sits in the middle of the sum. A till and a website would need the same rule, and copying it into each invites two different mistakes.

lesson.orientation: Trace branches, ranges, loop updates and Boolean conditions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A car park barrier has no attendant to ask how long you stayed. A small program reads the ticket, works out the fee and lifts the barrier. A stay under an hour costs £2 and a stay under three hours costs £5. Anything longer costs £9. Whoever wrote the program had to say what happens for each kind of stay, and the answer is different every time.

At closing time the same program has a second job. It must add up the fee from every car that came in that day, which means doing one small calculation once per car. Nobody wants to write the sum out three hundred times, so the program needs a way to say 'do this for every car' and another way to say 'keep going until the car park is full'.
This lesson follows the barrier program as it grows. It starts by choosing between fees. After that it learns to repeat work, and it ends by combining several yes-or-no tests into one decision.

intro.promise: By the end you'll trace which fee an if chain picks and how many times a loop repeats.

recap.keyIdea: A chain runs the first true branch, a for loop visits each item once, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass.

blocks.text: You followed the fee chain for a driver with 7 visits and found that it stops at the second branch, a fee of 2. The loop over range(3, 12, 3) ran 3 times and totalled 18. You also saw that 5 & 3 is 1, because the two numbers share only their last binary digit.

recap.nextHook: The fee rule now sits in the middle of the end-of-day program. A till, a report and a website all need the same rule, and a copy in each place is one more thing to forget when the prices change. The next lesson shows how to give a rule a name, so it is written once and called wherever it is needed.

questions.prompt: A fee is 0 when units >= 10, otherwise 2 when units >= 5, otherwise 4. What is the fee for 7 units?
hints: Stop at the first condition that holds.
Check units >= 10 before units >= 5.
For 7 units, follow the first true condition to its fee.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first condition is false and the second true, so the fee is 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The first condition fails for 7 and the second holds, so the chain stops there.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs 10 units or more. For 7 units the first condition fails.
That is the else branch. The second condition already held, so else never ran.

hints: The stop value is excluded.
Start at 2 and keep adding the step.
List the generated values below 9 and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The range contains 2, 4, 6 and 8; their sum is 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. The range holds 2, 4, 6 and 8, and sum adds them.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes 10. The range stops before 9.
Start the list at 2, not 3. Count 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.prompt: Start count = 0 and turns = 0. While count < 7, add 2 to count and add 1 to turns. What is turns at the end?
hints: Test the condition before each pass.
Write the values of count: 0, then 2, and so on.
Stop when count is no longer below 7, and count the passes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: count reaches 2, 4, 6 and 8, so the body ran 4 times.

questions.onCorrect: 4. count goes 2, 4, 6, 8. At 6 the test still passed, so one more pass ran.

misconceptions.feedback: At 6 the condition count < 7 is still true, so there is one more pass.
That is the final value of count. The question asks how many passes ran.

questions.prompt: With x = 6, how many of these are True: x > 3 and x < 9, x > 8 or x < 2, not x > 5?
hints: Work out each part separately, then combine them.
and needs both parts true. or needs one.
not flips True and False.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first is True; the second and third are False.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Only the first holds: 6 is above 3 and below 9. The other two come out False.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the third: x > 5 is True, so not x > 5 is False.
The first test holds: 6 is above 3 and below 9.
or needs one true part, and neither part of the second is true.

questions.prompt: Start x = 2. While x < 10, add 3 to x. What is x when the loop stops?
hints: Test the condition before each update.
Write the values: start at 2 and keep adding 3.
Stop after the first value that fails x < 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The updates produce 5, 8 and 11. At 11 the condition is false.

questions.onCorrect: 11. The values are 5, 8, then 11, and 11 fails the test, so the loop ends there.

misconceptions.feedback: At 8 the condition x < 10 still holds, so one more addition happens.
x never equals 10 here. It jumps from 8 over the limit.

questions.prompt: What is 5 & 3 when both operands are integers?
hints: Compare aligned binary digits.
Write both numbers in binary with the same width.
Keep only the bits that are set in both.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In binary, 5 is 101 and 3 is 011. Their shared set bit is 001, which is 1.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Written in binary, 5 and 3 share only the last bit.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. & compares their binary digits.
That is 5 × 3. & keeps only bits set in both numbers.

hints: Is 2 hours under 1 hour?
Is it under 3 hours?
Pick the first charge whose limit the stay fits under.
questions.prompt: What does a 2-hour stay cost, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 hours is not under 1 but is under 3, so the charge is £5.

questions.onCorrect: £5. Two hours is not under 1 hour but is under 3, so the second charge applies. An if chain checks in that order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the under-1-hour charge. A 2-hour stay is longer than that.
That is for longer than 3 hours. A 2-hour stay is shorter.

hints: Which sign is used to compare, and which to store?
questions.prompt: What does the single equals sign do in units = 5?

choices.label: Tests whether units is greater than 5

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A single = is an assignment; comparison uses ==.

questions.onCorrect: It stores 5 under the name units. Comparing two values takes a double equals sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Checking is done with a double equals sign. One sign stores a value.
Greater than is written with its own symbol. The single equals sign stores.

hints: Recall how slices treat their stop position.

choices.label: Only if a step is given

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stop value is not included in the range.

questions.onCorrect: No. range stops before its stop value, so range(2, 6) gives 2, 3, 4 and 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Like a slice, range includes its start and excludes its stop.
The step only sets the gap between values. The stop is always excluded.

hints: What would the total be before any item has been added?

choices.label: So the first item is added to nothing
So the loop knows when to stop

acceptedIdeas: So the first item is added to nothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Starting the total at 0 means nothing extra is included before the first item.

questions.onCorrect: A total starts at 0 so the first item is added to nothing and does not change the result.

misconceptions.feedback: This range started at 1. The 0 is for the running total, not the range.
The loop stops when the range is used up. The 0 is the starting total.

hints: List the values: begin at the start and add the step each time.
Stop before 12.
Count the values you listed.
questions.prompt: How many times does the loop run?
questions.onCorrect: 3. The range gives 3, 6 and 9, so the body runs once for each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts 12. The stop value is excluded.

hints: Add the items one by one to a total that starts at 0.
The items are 3, 6 and 9.
Work out 3 + 6 + 9.
questions.prompt: What is total at the end?
questions.onCorrect: 18. The loop added each item to total in turn.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes 12, which is excluded. The range stops before 12.
That is only the last item. The total adds every item.
